pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Reading and drawing circuit diagrams

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England, KS2 Year 6 Electricity, statutory):** 'use recognised symbols when representing a simple circuit in a diagram'; non-statutory note confirms recognised symbols are introduced at Year 6 (Year 4 draws circuits pictorially).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** US NATIONAL (NGSS): no direct grade-4/5 circuit-diagram performance expectation (UK-anchored).

- **Operational details:** Children read and draw simple circuit diagrams using standard symbols (cell, bulb/lamp, switch, buzzer, wire), judge from a diagram whether a circuit is complete or broken (switch open/closed → will the bulb light?), and match a diagram to the physical circuit it represents. The core representational idea: a circuit diagram is a SCHEMATIC CONVENTION — a map of what connects to what — NOT a literal picture of the layout; wires are drawn as straight lines. NOTE: in England recognised symbols are formally introduced in Year 6 (Year 4 uses pictorial drawings), so this sits at that transition. This representational skill underpins 'Drawing circuits with proper symbols' and reading circuit diagrams for the KS3 current/voltage work.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/representational, age 9-10).
bestPractices: Introduce each symbol as a name-tag for a real component the child has handled — map the physical bulb to its symbol — so the notation labels known objects, not abstractions.

Teach the schematic convention explicitly: wires are STRAIGHT lines, the diagram shows CONNECTIONS not physical positions, and it is read as a loop — contrast a tidy schematic with a messy 'picture' of the real wires.
Work both directions and matching: build a circuit then draw it; read a diagram and build it; and match a photo of a physical circuit to the correct diagram from a set (the Y6 evidence task).
Use the diagram to PREDICT behaviour: from the drawn switch (open/closed) decide whether the loop is complete and the bulb lights — tying the representation back to the complete-loop rule.
Distinguish the cell and battery symbols early (one long + one short line = a cell; repeated pairs = a battery; the long thin line is the positive end) to head off the commonest symbol slip.
keyRepresentations: A symbol key: cell, battery, bulb/lamp (cross-in-circle), switch (open and closed), buzzer, wire — each beside its real photo.
Photo↔diagram matching pairs (a physical circuit and its schematic).
A straight-line schematic contrasted with a curvy 'picture' of the same circuit to teach the convention.
Complete vs broken diagrams (switch open vs closed) for 'will it light?' reading.
commonMisconceptions: Diagram-as-picture: drawing curvy wires or arranging symbols to mimic the physical layout instead of a straight-line schematic of the connections (the same iconic-representation trap as graph-as-picture).
Cell vs battery symbol confusion — calling one cell 'a battery' or drawing the wrong number of line-pairs.
Ignoring which line is positive (the long thin line) / orientation of the cell symbol.
Reading a gap or an open switch in a diagram as 'still works' — not connecting open/broken in the diagram to the bulb not lighting.
Treating the diagram as exact scale/position — thinking the component drawn nearest the cell is special, rather than only the connections mattering.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, learners read and draw simple circuit diagrams using standard symbols (cell, battery, bulb/lamp, switch open/closed, buzzer, wire). The central representational idea is that a circuit diagram is a schematic convention — a map of what connects to what, drawn with straight wires — not a literal picture of the physical layout. Learners work in both directions (build then draw; read then build), match photographs of real circuits to the correct diagram, and use the drawn switch state to predict whether the loop is complete and the bulb lights. This connects the notation back to the complete-loop rule and heads off common symbol and reading slips.

activities.title: Build a circuit, then draw its diagram
feedback: If the learner draws little pictures (a battery drawing, a light-bulb picture) instead of symbols, pair each real component with its agreed symbol on a key card, then redraw using only symbols.
If the drawn parts are strung along an open line or end in a dead-end, trace the path aloud — it must return to the other terminal of the cell; close the loop.
When the second drawing (symbols moved, connections kept) is accepted as the same circuit, name the insight: position is free, connections are fixed.
activities.rationale: The standard requires using recognised symbols to represent a simple circuit, and producing a drawing (not just recognising symbols) exposes learners who cannot translate to a working loop. Building both directions ties the notation to a real, handled circuit.
sourceClaims: Y6 Electricity statutory requirement: 'use recognised symbols when representing a simple circuit in a diagram'; recognised symbols are introduced at Year 6 (Year 4 draws pictorially).
learnerActions: Build or examine a simple physical circuit with a cell, a switch and a bulb joined by wires.

Draw a circuit diagram of it using only standard symbols: cell (one long thin line + one short thicker line, long line = positive terminal), bulb/lamp (cross-in-circle), switch (drawn open as a gap/lever or closed, matching the real switch), a buzzer symbol only if the circuit includes a buzzer, and wires as straight lines.
Trace the drawn loop with a finger to check it returns to the other terminal of the cell — close any open or dead-end path.
Redraw the same circuit a second time placing the symbols in different positions on the page but keeping the same connections, then confirm it represents the same circuit.
activities.intendedInsight: A circuit diagram records connections, not physical positions or appearance: where you put a symbol on the page does not matter, only what it joins to. The drawing must form a single closed loop back to the cell.

activities.title: Straight-line schematic vs curvy picture
feedback: If the learner keeps wires curved to 'look like' the real wires, point out that the schematic is a map of connections, not a photo of the layout — straighten the wires without changing what joins to what.
If the learner thinks the component drawn nearest the cell is special, have them redraw with that component moved further away but still connected — the circuit behaves identically.
activities.rationale: Treating a schematic as a literal picture is a recurring representational error akin to graph-as-picture confusion; directly contrasting the two forms targets that convention.
sourceClaims: Treating a schematic as a literal picture (drawing wires to mimic physical layout) is a recurring representational error, of a kind with iconic graph-as-picture confusion.
learnerActions: Look at a 'picture-style' drawing of a circuit where the wires are drawn curvy to mimic the real tangle of leads.
Redraw the same circuit as a tidy schematic: straight-line wires and standard symbols.
Check that both represent the same circuit by tracing each loop and confirming the same components are connected in the same order.
State in your own words why both 'work' even though they look different.
activities.intendedInsight: A tidy straight-line schematic and a messy curvy picture of the same connections describe the same circuit; the schematic convention (straight wires, standard symbols) makes the connections easy to read without implying anything about physical shape or layout.

activities.title: Read the switch and predict: will the bulb light?
feedback: If the learner reads an open (gap) switch as closed ('the line's there, so it's on'), line up the open-switch symbol beside a real open switch and the closed one beside a closed switch; a gap means a broken loop means no light.
If the learner says a diagram with a break will still light, have them trace the loop and find where it fails to return to the cell.
activities.rationale: Using the diagram to predict behaviour ties the representation back to the physical complete-loop rule and surfaces learners who misread switch state. This is one of the stated evidence outcomes for the topic, though the complete-loop rule itself is not quoted in the cited sources.
learnerActions: Examine a diagram and identify each symbol and what it stands for.
Decide whether the switch is drawn open (a gap/lever breaking the line) or closed, and say how you can tell.
Predict whether the bulb lights, giving the reason: the bulb lights only if the loop is complete, which requires the switch to be closed.
Redraw the switch in its other state and re-predict.
Given a diagram with a break in the loop just after the bulb, predict whether it lights, then redraw it so it does.
activities.intendedInsight: An open switch or any gap in the drawn loop means a broken loop, so the bulb does not light; reading the diagram's switch state connects the notation directly to the complete-loop rule.

activities.title: Match the photo to the diagram
feedback: If a learner cannot justify the rejection of distractors, have them trace the loop in each diagram and compare, component by component, with the photo.
Confirm success when the learner names the ruling-out detail, not just the correct match.
activities.rationale: Matching a photograph of a physical circuit to the correct diagram is a stated Year 6 evidence outcome and assesses the reading/translation skill. A tappable key and linked photo/diagram panels make the reference layer concrete, but these are optional supports, not required mechanisms. The matching outcome is not the content of the quoted statutory claim, so no source is cited for the principle.
learnerActions: Look at a photograph of a real physical circuit.
Choose, from a set of candidate diagrams, the one that matches it.
Say which specific detail rules out each of the other options (e.g. a missing connection, wrong switch state, an extra component).

Where available, use a tappable symbol key (tap a symbol to see its name, a photo of the real component, and what it does) and a side-by-side photo/diagram view with linked parts as a reference while deciding.
activities.intendedInsight: Translating fluently between a physical circuit, a photograph and a schematic depends on matching connections rather than surface appearance; justifying the rejected options forces attention to the connections that distinguish circuits.

activities.title: Cell vs battery, and which line is positive
feedback: If the learner calls one cell 'a battery' or draws the wrong number of pairs, show the one-pair cell beside the repeated-pairs battery and have them count.
If orientation/positive end is ignored, have them label the long thin line as positive on each of their own drawings.
activities.rationale: Cell-vs-battery confusion and ignoring which line is positive are identified common misconceptions; a dedicated discrimination and spot-the-error task targets them. No cited source.claim directly states this discrimination principle, so no source is attributed.
learnerActions: Study the cell symbol (one long thin line and one short line) and the battery symbol (repeated line-pairs).
Identify which line is the positive terminal (the long thin line).
Draw a single cell, then draw a battery of two cells, labelling the positive end.
Spot the error: given a few diagrams, find the one that draws the wrong number of line-pairs or mislabels/omits the positive end, and correct it.
activities.intendedInsight: A single cell and a multi-cell battery have distinct symbols, and the long thin line marks the positive terminal; getting this right avoids a common symbol slip.

constraints: Learners must produce their own diagrams (draw and construct), not only recognise or select symbols; recognition-only tasks do not themselves elicit independent construction of a working loop.

A tappable symbol key and linked photo/diagram panels are useful reference and matching supports, but they cannot host the learner's own drawing; pair them with an activity that requires constructing a diagram.

An interactive editor that lights the on-canvas bulb only when the loop is complete and the switch closed is a strong optional way to give immediate feedback and reveal that symbol position is free while connections are fixed; it is a proposal, not a required medium. Pairing with a real build-then-draw activity is a natural complement.

Keep diagrams flat: the whole point is that spatial position does not matter, only connections. A 3D treatment is not recommended because it works against this idea; this is a scope judgement for this topic, not a universal claim about 3D.
This sits at the England transition where recognised symbols are formally introduced in Year 6 (Year 4 uses pictorial drawings); learners may arrive expecting to draw pictures.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's one IOP Spark source on schematic-as-picture error is marked verified:false in the source data; the comparison to graph-as-picture confusion should be treated as an illustrative analogy, not established efficacy.

The legacy entry asserted that dialogue 'adds little' and that 3D 'works against' the concept; these are scoped design judgements, not established comparative efficacy. A conversation can still support teaching the convention, and the 3D note is retained only as a topic-scope preference.

SourceClaims on the predict-lighting, photo-matching, and cell-vs-battery activities were set to [] because the quoted statutory claim directly supports representing a circuit with symbols, not the complete-loop prediction, matching, or cell/battery-discrimination principles; those remain research-informed outcomes without a directly supporting source.claim.

Self-audit: the complete-loop reasoning (open switch or any gap = broken loop = bulb off; closed complete loop = bulb on) and the cell-symbol convention (long thin line = positive, one pair = cell, repeated pairs = battery) are internally consistent with the source and retained as taught.

probeDeeper: Point to the switch symbol — is it open or closed, and how can you tell? Now draw the OTHER state.
Here's a photo of a real circuit and three diagrams. Which diagram matches, and which detail rules the others out?
In your drawing, trace the loop with your finger — does it come back to the cell?
Counterexample: I draw the bulb symbol with a break in the loop just after it. Will it light? Redraw it so it does.
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the symbols correctly (long/short parallel lines = cell terminals, circle-with-cross = bulb, gap or lever = switch), states whether the switch is open (gap) or closed, and predicts the bulb lights only if the loop is complete and the switch closed. Then draws a correct single-loop diagram: cell, closed-switch symbol and bulb joined by straight lines into a closed loop.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws little pictures — a battery drawing, a light-bulb picture — instead of the standard symbols ('I'll just draw what it looks like').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Match each real component to its agreed symbol on a key card, then redraw using only symbols.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The production step yields pictorial drawings, not symbols.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the switch symbol — reads an open (gap) switch as closed, so predicts the bulb lights when it wouldn't ('the line's there, so it's on').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up the open-switch symbol beside a real open switch and the closed one beside a closed switch; a gap = broken loop = no light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gets the open/closed reading and the lighting prediction wrong.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws components strung along an open line or a dead-end rather than a closed loop ('a row of parts').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the drawn path — it must return to the other terminal; close the loop.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The drawn diagram doesn't form a complete loop back to the cell.

responseLevels.gap: Draws pictorial components or open/dead-end arrangements, or misreads the open/closed switch.
responseLevels.full: Reads each symbol and the switch state to predict lighting, and produces a correct closed-loop diagram in standard symbols, translating fluently between physical circuit, photo and diagram.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and draws standard symbols but makes a translation slip — misreads switch state, the drawn loop isn't quite closed, or can't match photo to diagram confidently.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a circuit diagram. First, tell me what each symbol stands for and what this circuit would do — in particular, is the switch open or closed, and will the bulb light? Then draw me the diagram for a circuit with a cell, a closed switch and a bulb in a single loop.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking the child to READ (what does this symbol mean?) and then PRODUCE (now draw one) exposes those who recognise symbols passively but can't translate to a working loop, who draw pictures instead of symbols, or who misread the open/closed switch.
